body: @nzakas Can you take another look at this issue? I'm not sure this is an issue we want to address–the requested functionality doesn't match JSHint's treatment of their _quotmark_ rule.

I think this is a valid issue. It's very common to mix quotes to avoid escaping. So I think this is a right thing to add, in a long run. However, I'm not sure if this is necessary right now for version 0.1.0.
Perhaps this should be an option on the `quotes` rule or an alternative rule, rather than a bugfix?
I would go with an option, I guess, since creating identical rule just to check for small difference seems redundant.
I've re-read this a  few times and I'm still unclear on what the desired behavior is and how it is different from what happens already. Can someone summarize?

@nzakas Right now the `quotes` rule functionality is that if you specify `quotes: [1, "double"]`, ESLint will warn on _any_ string literal that is single-quoted. Likewise if you specify `quotes: [1, 'single']`, ESLint will warn on _any_ string literal that is double-quoted.

The proposed functionality is the if you specify `quotes: [1, "double"]`, and ESLint finds a single-quoted string it will only warn if there are no double-quotes _inside_ the string. 

So, to illustrate:

``` js
// Current functionality for quotes: [1, "double"]
var foo = "this is \"my\" string"  // pass
var foo = 'this is "my" string'  // warn

// Proposed functionality for quotes: [1, "double"]
var foo = "this is \"my\" string"  // pass
var foo = 'this is "my" string'  // pass, because double quotes found inside
```
Thanks for the explanation. I'm not sold on this change - someone convince me.

@nzakas I think the argument in favor of this feature goes something like this:

It is common enough for a programmer to reverse their normal quote style to avoid quote escaping, that it makes sense to have an _option_ on the `quotes` rule to make it more lax in these situations. In addition, avoiding quote escaping saves the programmer one character per would've-been-escaped-quote in the file. And lastly, escaped quotes can add visual noise to a string, decreasing readability.

My skepticism is because I've never encountered this convention before in my career - and I've seen a lot of weird stuff. I can maybe see adding it as another option, but definitely not as default behavior. I guess my big question is if this is common enough that it should be baked in?

Hmm.. I have an opposite experience. I almost never seen people escaping quotes unless they absolutely have to. You can just take a look at our own test cases. Almost every test case has mixed quotes in it, since it's a pain to escape them. I would suggest adding it as an option to the quotes rule.
@ilyavolodin okay, I can buy adding it as another option that is off by default.
:+1: on @ilyavolodin's use case. I find it more common to see alternating quotes in that case vs escaping.

I implemented this last night in my local repo and have a couple of questions:
1. What would be a good name for this option? I've used `allowAvoidEscape`, but I think it is a poor name.
2. Is there any objection to rules taking keyword arguments such as `{ quote: "double", allowAvoidEscape: true }`? I believe using them makes the rule config more readable and extensible but will switch to discrete arguments if desired.

@brandonpayton 
We discussed options as objects before, and decided against it. While it might be slightly easier to ready, it's just not necessary. Also, from your example above, it's not clear if the rule is enabled or disabled, and if it's set as a error or warning. I think we should stick to the existing way of setting options, i.e. array of values.
Quote rule already have an option, that can be set to either "double" or "single", I think you have a choice, of either adding another option, like this:
`"quote": [2, "double", true]`
or having 4 options, like this:
`"quote": [2, "double-outer"]`

I'd opt more for a string than a boolean, since a boolean doesn't tell you
what's going on:

"quote": [ 2, "double", "something-descriptive" ]
